label: Mandir
signOff: Regular Attendee, SKS Swaminarayan Temple Woolwich
subject: Objection to Proposed School Street Traffic Regulation
body:
Dear School Streets Traffic Regulation Order Team,

Re: Objection to Proposed School Street Traffic Regulation Order (TRO) on St Margaret’s Grove, Plumstead, London SE18 7RL / TMO Number T8(26)

I am writing to formally object to the proposed School Street scheme on St. Margarets Grove, as a regular attendee of SKS Swaminarayan Temple Woolwich, which is located within the affected zone.

While I support the underlying aims of improving child safety, I believe the current proposal fails to adequately consider the essential accessibility needs of our congregation and will have a severe and disproportionate impact on elderly, disabled and vulnerable members of our community.

My primary grounds for objection are outlined below:

1. Severe Impact on Elderly and Disabled Attendees

Many of our worshippers are elderly, have mobility impairments, or live with hidden disabilities. For these individuals, walking long distances from outside the restricted zone is simply not practical or physically possible.

Requiring them to park some distance away effectively prevents them from attending daily services, morning and evening prayers, and important community gatherings. The scheme creates a significant barrier to religious practice and community participation for those with physical limitations.

2. Disruption to Community and Faith Services

SKS Swaminarayan Temple Woolwich is not merely a place of worship; it is a vital community hub providing religious, educational, social and wellbeing services. It offers social support, activities for children, families, retirees and vulnerable members of the community.

The proposed restriction times directly overlap with key worship periods and community service activities.

Restricting vehicle access will impede the transportation of elderly and frail members who depend on family members or volunteers for transport.

It will also affect volunteers, visitors and the delivery of essential supplies required for the Temple's day-to-day operations.

3. Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) Concerns

Under the Equality Act 2010, public authorities have a duty to give due regard to the impact of their decisions on people with protected characteristics, including age, disability and religion or belief.

In its current form, the proposal risks indirect discrimination by significantly restricting access to a place of worship without providing adequate mitigation or reasonable adjustments. It is our understanding that the accessibility needs of these protected groups have not been fully assessed or properly addressed before progressing with this proposal.

4. Financial Burden and Reduced Accessibility

A significant number of attendees, particularly elderly residents, families with young children and people with limited mobility, rely on private vehicles to attend religious services, community activities and support programmes.

Public transport accessibility in this area is relatively limited, with the area around SE18 7RL understood to have a Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) of approximately 2, making access by public transport less convenient for many users.

The introduction of parking permits and associated costs would therefore place an unnecessary financial burden on members of our community. For some individuals and families, these additional costs may discourage or prevent regular attendance at religious services and community events.

This would have wider implications for:
Wellbeing and mental health.
Social inclusion, particularly for elderly and isolated residents.
Access to important religious, educational and community support services provided by the Temple.

These broader community impacts should be carefully considered before any final decision is made.

Conclusion

I respectfully ask the Council to reconsider the current proposal, undertake a more comprehensive Equality Impact Assessment.

Thank you for considering my objection and do not implement the Traffic Regulation Order.

Yours faithfully,

[Your name]
Regular Attendee, SKS Swaminarayan Temple Woolwich

label: Nursery
subject: Objection to Proposed School Street Traffic Regulation
body:
Dear School Streets Traffic Regulation Order Team,

Re: Objection to Proposed School Street Traffic Regulation Order (TRO) on St Margaret’s Grove, Plumstead, London SE18 7RL / TMO Number T8(26)

I am writing to formally object to the proposed School Street scheme on St. Margarets Grove, as a parent/carer of a child attending Bal Krishna Nursery at SKS Swaminarayan Temple Woolwich, which is located within the affected zone.

While I support the underlying aims of improving child safety, I believe the current proposal fails to adequately consider the essential access needs of nursery families and will have a severe and disproportionate impact on young children, working parents and carers, and those who rely on vehicle access for drop-off and pick-up.

My primary grounds for objection are outlined below:

1. Severe Impact on Nursery Drop-off and Pick-up

Bal Krishna Nursery cares for children aged 2 to 5. At this age, children cannot reasonably walk long distances to and from the setting, particularly in poor weather, while families are also managing bags, pushchairs, car seats, younger siblings and nursery belongings.

Drop-off and pick-up windows are short and time-critical. Many parents and carers are travelling to or from work and cannot add a long walk at both ends of the nursery day.

Requiring families to park outside the restricted zone and walk in with small children is simply not practical. It creates a significant barrier to accessing early years childcare and would make regular attendance far more difficult for many families.

2. Disruption to Working Families and Child Safety

The proposed restriction times are likely to overlap with peak nursery drop-off and pick-up periods.

Restricting vehicle access will impede parents, carers and grandparents who transport young children to the nursery, including those with more than one child, those with mobility needs, and those using buggies and car seats.

It will also affect nursery staff arriving for shifts, visitors, and the delivery of food and other essential supplies required for the nursery's day-to-day operations.

Displaced parking and longer walking routes with toddlers at the busiest times of day risk increasing, rather than reducing, road safety problems around the site.

3. Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) Concerns

Under the Equality Act 2010, public authorities have a duty to give due regard to the impact of their decisions on people with protected characteristics, including age, disability, sex, and religion or belief.

In its current form, the proposal risks indirect discrimination by significantly restricting access to an early years setting used by very young children and their families, without providing adequate mitigation or reasonable adjustments. Nursery-age children, pregnant women and new mothers, disabled parents and carers, and families using a faith-based community nursery would be particularly affected.

It is our understanding that these accessibility and childcare needs have not been fully assessed or properly addressed before progressing with this proposal.

4. Limited Alternatives and Wider Family Impact

A significant number of families rely on private vehicles for nursery drop-off and pick-up because of work schedules, multiple children, distance from home, and the practical realities of travelling with toddlers.

Public transport accessibility in this area is relatively limited, with the area around SE18 7RL understood to have a Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) of approximately 2. Buses and walking are often impractical for a timed nursery drop-off with young children.

The need to park further away, or to obtain permits and meet associated costs, would place an unnecessary burden on working families. For some, these barriers may discourage or prevent regular nursery attendance.

This would have wider implications for:
Access to childcare and early years education.
Parents' and carers' ability to work and commute.
The wellbeing of young children and families.
Social inclusion for families who rely on this local nursery.

These broader family and community impacts should be carefully considered before any final decision is made.

Conclusion

I respectfully ask the Council to reconsider the current proposal, undertake a more comprehensive Equality Impact Assessment, and not implement the Traffic Regulation Order without proper provision for nursery drop-off and pick-up.

Thank you for considering my objection.

Yours faithfully,

[Your name]
Parent/Carer, Bal Krishna Nursery
